justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 56.4 at the one-day mark and rising gradually to 57.5 at one month. This trajectory likely reflects a base assumption of mild positive momentum or mean-reversion from a slightly depressed current level, combined with whatever fundamental or technical anchor was relevant at the time of the forecast. The one-day estimate is essentially anchored to the last observed value with very little expected movement, while the one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a small positive drift that could reflect things like earnings expectations, macroeconomic tailwinds, or a broader market trend that was in place when the forecast was made.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a standard reflection of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 1.2 units, consistent with the relatively predictable short-term behavior of most financial or economic series where large overnight moves are uncommon. By one week, the interval widens to 6.6 units, capturing the possibility of meaningful news events, data releases, or sentiment shifts. At one month, the interval spans 15 units, acknowledging that over a four-week window almost anything can happen — policy changes, earnings surprises, geopolitical shocks, or shifts in sector rotation could all move the outcome significantly in either direction.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include tail events that were not well-represented in historical data at the time of the forecast. On the downside, a sudden risk-off episode, a negative macro data surprise, or a liquidity event could push the value well below 50. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst — a strong earnings beat, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic — could push the value above 65. These fat-tail scenarios are precisely why the one-month interval is wide, but even so, truly extreme events could breach those bounds.

It is also worth noting that my estimates carry model uncertainty on top of the stated statistical uncertainty. The forecast assumed a relatively stable regime, but if the underlying data-generating process shifts — for instance, if volatility clustering intensifies or correlations across assets break down — then the confidence intervals themselves could be miscalibrated. In short, the intervals represent my best attempt at capturing plausible outcomes, but they should not be treated as hard bounds on what is possible.
